items.title: OpenAI publishes new mathematical results from internal frontier model with Lean proof formalizations and research details on GitHub [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI has released a collection of new mathematical findings generated by an internal frontier AI model, sharing formalized proofs in the Lean programming language and detailed research data on GitHub. The release follows consultations with the Institute for Advanced Study's Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence to establish best practices for sharing such results. The GitHub repository includes protocols for paper revisions, citations, summaries of the model's reasoning, compute usage estimates equivalent to about three hours of ChatGPT Pro per result, and statistics on problem attempts. OpenAI plans to fund workshops and programs to further explore AI-produced mathematical advancements and aims to responsibly release the model while continuing to refine disclosure standards based on community feedback.

items.title: Simon Willison tests Mistral Large 4 and other AI models generating SVGs of an armadillo in fishnet tights jaywalking on Mars [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Simon Willison shared a comment on Hacker News about the saturation of AI benchmarks, illustrating this by prompting several large language models, including Mistral Large 4, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT 6.1 Sol, and Gemini 3.8 Flash, to generate SVG images of an armadillo in fishnet tights jaywalking on Mars. This playful test highlights the current state of frontier AI models and their reasoning capabilities. The results and default reasoning levels for each model are available through an online tool that renders the generated SVGs, providing a comparative look at how these advanced models handle creative and unusual prompts. This commentary reflects ongoing discussions about AI model evaluation and benchmarking in the community.

items.title: Strands releases Decider 2B, an open-source 2 billion parameter decision model optimized for fast, local AI experimentation and agentic workflows [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Strands has introduced Decider 2B, a small decision model designed for rapid experimentation and local development in agentic AI. Unlike large language models that generate text, this model selects from predefined options with high accuracy and low latency, making it suitable for tasks requiring quick, reliable decisions rather than complex reasoning or text generation. Decider 2B is built by fine-tuning a pre-trained language model torso with a new pointer head that scores answer options, achieving competitive accuracy and calibration on benchmarks. It runs efficiently on common hardware, delivering responses in around 115 milliseconds on an Nvidia RTX3090 and slightly slower on consumer laptops. Strands has open-sourced the model, training data, and scripts on GitHub and Hugging Face to encourage community innovation in decision-focused AI models.

items.title: HUMXN launches free plumbing and HVAC service program in Minnesota to collect AI training data from skilled labor [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: HUMXN, an AI data and training company, has started a program offering free plumbing, electrical, HVAC, air-duct cleaning, and carpet-cleaning services in Minneapolis, Chicago, and Miami. The initiative uses wearable capture technology on technicians to record real-world skilled labor tasks, creating datasets for AI and robotics development. The program subsidizes these home-service appointments by turning the technicians' work into valuable training data, benefiting homeowners with free services, paying service companies, and providing AI developers with authentic examples of physical problem-solving. HUMXN plans to expand this model to more markets and service categories as demand for physical-world AI training data grows.

items.title: Claix.dev develops an alternative to traditional vector-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation for AI agent memory, emphasizing agent-controlled retrieval workflows [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Claix.dev presents a new approach to Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) tailored for AI agents, shifting from fixed vector-based retrieval pipelines to agentic RAG where agents dynamically decide when and how to retrieve information. This method addresses limitations of traditional RAG, such as loss of document structure from chunking, semantic similarity not equating to business relevance, and the need for multi-step retrieval processes in complex workflows. The alternative approach highlights that vector databases and embeddings remain useful but should not be the default architecture for all AI agents. Instead, retrieval becomes an active tool within the agent's decision-making process, allowing for more flexible, multi-step interactions with external information sources. This design aims to better support AI agents performing tasks that require iterative reasoning, tool use, and evaluation beyond simple question answering.

items.title: OpenAI adds College Planner and new learning tools to ChatGPT for Teens, including a teen AI council, to support college preparation and AI education [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI is expanding ChatGPT for Teens with a College Planner feature designed to help high school students in grades 10-12 manage college applications, deadlines, and financial aid steps. The update also introduces new study tools and a teen AI council to engage young users in AI learning and planning. The College Planner consolidates application requirements and timelines for multiple schools, allowing students to track progress and ask ChatGPT questions about the process. OpenAI is partnering with the College Advising Corps to support under-resourced high schools and plans to extend College Planner support to more countries and educational paths over time. Early usage data shows teens actively use ChatGPT for learning, with millions engaging in study-related activities and taking breaks as recommended. OpenAI aims to continue refining the experience based on feedback from teens, families, and educators to make AI tools more accessible and supportive for young learners.

items.title: Healthleap raises $38M to expand AI platform that identifies hospital patients at risk of undiagnosed conditions, deployed in over 50 hospitals [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Healthleap, a startup founded in South Africa in 2022, has raised $38 million in seed and Series A funding to develop its AI platform that analyzes patient records to flag hospital patients who may need closer medical review. The platform uses language models to extract clinical information from doctors' notes and combines it with structured data to identify risks such as malnutrition and delirium, without diagnosing patients directly. The company's AI is currently used in more than 50 hospitals, including Penn Medicine and Cedars-Sinai, screening for multiple conditions and showing significant financial impact, such as $23.8 million in annualized savings at the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania. Healthleap plans to use the funding to enhance its technology, expand condition coverage, and enter outpatient and home care markets.

items.title: Mumsnet denies using AI to generate forum content after AI prompt appears on message board [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Mumsnet has denied using artificial intelligence to write posts on its popular forum after a detailed AI prompt appeared in response to a user seeking advice. The prompt included instructions for generating a typical "am I being unreasonable" post, causing users to question the site's use of AI for content creation. The prompt was initially explained by Mumsnet as coming from a tool that suggests thread titles using an OpenAI model, but users remained skeptical and speculated it leaked from internal systems. Mumsnet's founder confirmed the prompt originated from their system due to an error but reiterated that AI is not used to write threads or replies, emphasizing that forum content is created by real users.

items.title: Meta launches Muse AI agent with native iPad support and releases Mac version, expanding its AI assistant across Apple devices [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Meta has updated its Muse AI agent app to include native support for the iPad, optimizing it for the larger screen and multitasking features of iPadOS. This update follows the app's initial launch nearly a month ago, during which it became the top free app in Apple's App Store. A Mac version of Muse was also released shortly after the original mobile debut, extending its functionality to desktop tasks such as file organization. The new iPad version offers similar features to the iPhone app but is designed to better utilize the iPad's capabilities. Additional updates include integrations with software tools like Canva, Dropbox, and Zoom, targeting small business users with autonomous marketing and product development planning features. Meta's quicker rollout of Muse for iPad compared to its Instagram iPad app reflects the company's strong focus on AI initiatives, which also include plans for a standalone Muse device and integration with smart glasses.

items.title: Pentagon's Tradewinds program speeds AI procurement with five-minute product videos, enabling faster contracts with companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: The Department of Defense's Tradewinds initiative aims to accelerate AI technology acquisitions by allowing companies to submit brief five-minute videos showcasing their products. Accepted submissions gain a "post-competitive" status that helps government buyers bypass lengthy procurement processes, sometimes securing contracts in under a week. Managed by the DoD's Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office, Tradewinds targets nontraditional defense contractors and focuses on strategic AI areas such as enhancing force lethality and AI-enabled targeting agents. The program leverages flexible contracting methods like "other transaction" agreements, which can expedite deals but have raised concerns about oversight and transparency, prompting recent legislative efforts to increase reporting requirements.

items.title: Tony Fadell says first wave of AI gadgets failed to solve real problems and stresses need for trust in next generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Tony Fadell, known as the "father of the iPod," criticized early AI gadgets like the Rabbit R1 and Humane AI pin for failing to meet real consumer needs and lacking practical utility. He emphasized that most people have never had a personal assistant and thus do not know how to use or trust AI assistants effectively. Fadell highlighted that building trust with AI assistants is crucial, especially regarding privacy and security, and suggested that successful AI agents will need to operate primarily on-device to protect sensitive data. He noted that Apple, with its hardware ecosystem and user trust, is well-positioned to lead in this space despite currently relying on external AI models for Siri. Fadell also pointed out that companies without access to widespread hardware are creating standalone AI devices to gather sensor data, which raises additional privacy concerns.

items.title: AI leaders from Nebius, Uber, and NVIDIA discuss optimizing AI compute efficiency by shifting from token maxing to value maxing, using tailored inference platforms, caching, and data management [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: A recent panel featuring AI leaders from Nebius, Uber, and NVIDIA explored strategies to improve compute efficiency amid growing token consumption from agentic workflows. They discussed approaches like speculative decoding, caching, and providing engineers with usage visibility to optimize performance and cost-effectiveness. Panelists emphasized that improving AI compute economics requires collaboration across the industry, combining hardware advances with software optimizations and data discipline. Uber highlighted its internal context graph to reduce query times and token use, while Nebius focuses on tailoring inference platforms to customer goals. The discussion also touched on evolving pricing models, with Nebius open to outcome-based pricing and anticipating more managed services to optimize workload routing in the near future.

items.title: Google Labs launches Playground, an AI-powered platform for creating browser-based games using text prompts, initially available in the U.S. for users 18 and older [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Google Labs has introduced Playground, an AI-driven game creation platform that enables users to build 2D or 3D browser games by describing gameplay and visuals through simple text prompts, without coding skills. Users can choose game genres, upload visuals for AI asset generation, and publish or share their games, which support features like leaderboards and multiplayer modes. Playground games are playable on mobile and desktop devices, with a free browsing experience and a token-based system for game generation; Google One AI subscribers receive higher usage limits. The platform plans to integrate Unity Spark for enhanced 3D capabilities and professional-level mechanics, and Google intends to expand Playground's availability beyond the U.S. in the future.

items.title: OpenAI's Alexander Embiricos to discuss new AI agent Dots at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 days after its launch [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Alexander Embiricos, product lead for OpenAI's new AI agent Dots, will speak at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 in San Francisco shortly after the product's launch. Dots are designed as always-on personal AI agents that operate autonomously, connect to everyday apps, and work continuously toward user goals. Embiricos will explore the future of AI agents beyond chatbots, addressing issues of autonomy, privacy, and trust in AI systems. His session, "What Comes After the Chatbot?", will be part of a broader event featuring over 250 tech leaders and 200 sessions focused on emerging technology trends.

items.title: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 announces full lineup of interactive roundtables featuring industry leaders from Nvidia, Chime, Anthropic, and others [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 will host over 10,000 founders, investors, and tech leaders in San Francisco from October 13-15, featuring interactive roundtables on topics including AI, fundraising, enterprise software, and physical AI. The event offers discounted passes and opportunities for attendees to engage directly with experts and peers on current industry challenges. The roundtables cover diverse subjects such as AI's impact on legacy industries, IPO readiness with AI-enabled finance, specialized AI training data, and the future of commerce AI. Sessions will be led by notable figures including CEOs, investors, and founders from companies like Smartsheet, Chime, and Base10 Partners, providing practical insights and networking opportunities for participants.

items.title: Google launches SynthID website to verify AI-generated images, videos, and audio across multiple formats [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Google has launched a new website that allows users to verify whether images, videos, or audio clips are AI-generated using its SynthID technology. The tool supports a wide range of media formats and is now publicly accessible after being tested by journalists and researchers since last year. SynthID watermarks media created by Google's AI models and tools like Gemini, Flow, and ProducerAI, and is also supported by OpenAI, Nvidia, and Kakao, with Apple expected to add support soon. Google integrates SynthID verification into its Gemini app and Chrome browser, handling about one million verification requests daily, while other companies like Microsoft and Meta use different watermarking standards that are not always reliable.

items.title: OpenAI launches Decisions API for faster yes/no, category, and scale evaluations at $0.10 per million input tokens [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI has introduced the Decisions API, which processes text and images about ten times faster than its previous Responses API and provides simplified outputs such as yes/no probabilities, category selections, or scale ratings. The API currently supports the gpt-6-luna model, is in public beta, and charges $0.10 per million input tokens with free output tokens. OpenAI has also streamlined its paid API tiers from five to three, with usage limits ranging from $500 to $200,000 per month.

items.title: Google DeepMind, Meta, and Isomorphic Labs invest $300 million in Mark Zuckerberg's Biohub to develop AI datasets for creating a virtual cell model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Google DeepMind, Meta, and AI drug discovery startup Isomorphic Labs are jointly investing $300 million into Biohub, the nonprofit biomedical research organization founded by Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan. This funding is part of a larger $1.8 billion initiative aimed at building AI datasets to enable researchers to digitally simulate biological processes and accelerate disease prevention and management. Biohub, established in 2016, focuses on creating a virtual cell to allow digital experimentation in biology. The effort also receives over $500 million in funding from the US Department of Energy and additional support from the National Institutes of Health through datasets and knowledge bases. Biohub's head of science, Alex Rives, emphasized that an accurate predictive model of biology could significantly speed up scientific discovery by enabling digital experiments, requiring coordinated data generation at national and international levels.

items.content_text: Elon Musk announced that SpaceX's AI unit will occasionally use AI models from competitors, such as Claude, to power its Grok Bot instead of relying solely on in-house models. This marks a shift in SpaceX's approach to selecting backend AI models based on task suitability rather than exclusive internal development.

items.title: Mistral launches Le Chonk, a 1 trillion-parameter open-weight AI model aimed at competing with top proprietary models in coding and cyberdefense [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: French AI company Mistral has released a preview of Le Chonk, a 1 trillion-parameter open-weight model designed to rival leading AI models from the US and China. The model targets specialized domains such as coding, cyberdefense, manufacturing, and finance, and is expected to have a final release by the end of the month. Mistral emphasizes that Le Chonk was trained from scratch rather than through distillation and positions it as the most capable open-weight model developed outside China. The company aims to provide a competitive alternative to proprietary models, especially amid growing geopolitical tensions and restrictions on AI access from US labs. Mistral generates revenue through cloud usage fees and engineering services, and recently raised $3.3 billion in funding at a $24 billion valuation.

items.title: Former Tesla Optimus Lead is Launching an Industrial Robot Startup [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Ashish Kumar, a former AI lead for Tesla's Optimus humanoid robots, has co-founded a startup developing non-humanoid robots that handle a variety of tasks that would normally be done by highly skilled workers in industries such as manufacturing and aerospace, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. The San Francisco startup, Intelligent Machines, has hired several former members of Tesla's Optimus team and is in the process of raising a seed round that could end up around $100 million, said one of the people. Intelligent Machines is currently focused on developing software for robots, but its leaders have discussed designing the hardware as well. The company uses reinforcement learning-a method that rewards AI for accomplishing certain goals and penalizes it for other actions-to teach robots to perform complex tasks, according to the two people. (Kumar's doctoral research at the University of California, Berkeley, focused on RL.)

items.title: Where Nvidia's $100 Billion Dealmaking Juggernaut Will Go Next [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: This July, Nvidia caught wind of a looming takeover of OpenRouter, a three-year-old startup that had emerged as a popular marketplace for AI models, including many cheaper open-source ones. Databricks and Stripe had already been talking to the startup about a potential sale. Nvidia was late to the party. The chipmaker's CEO, Jensen Huang, wanted in. Nvidia executives told their counterparts at OpenRouter they were interested and were prepared to make a generous offer, but they needed more time to evaluate a possible transaction before doing so, said a person with knowledge of the discussion. OpenRouter's founders didn't want to wait. Ultimately, Nvidia-whose interest in the startup hasn't previously been reported-didn't make a formal offer, and Stripe prevailed with an $8 billion bid for OpenRouter. Nvidia's dealmakers quickly moved on to other prizes. Over the next two months, they inked more than $140 billion worth of deals-including a $105 billion credit guarantee. The company held nearly $100 billion worth of equity investments and $25 billion in future investment commitments as of late July. More deals are likely.

items.title: Grab Redesigns Counter Service Storage for 50% Lower P99 Latency
items.content_text: Grab migrated its high-volume Counter Service from a wide column database to Aerospike using storage abstraction, shadow traffic, data parity validation, and gradual traffic migration. The redesigned data model consolidated time buckets into map-based records. Grab reports about 50% lower production p99 read latency, 1 TB versus 3 TB of disk usage, and 45% to 50% lower cost per node. By Leela Kumili

items.title: How much of AutoResearch is research, and how much is search?[D] [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: I've recently been working part-time on an AutoResearch-style project. The setup is roughly: humans take recent work from top-tier ML/AI conferences, turn part of it into a well-defined task with an evaluator, and then let an agent iteratively modify the solution and search for a better score. Working on this made me question what exactly we are evaluating. Once humans have already chosen the problem, defined the objective, designed the evaluator, and provided the initial research direction, the agent is mostly searching within a space that has already been heavily shaped for it. That search can still be useful. An agent may explore far more variants than a researcher would manually. But I'm less sure that score improvement alone captures what we usually mean by research sense. A researcher also asks whether a result reveals a general principle, whether it transfers, whether the problem formulation itself should change, or whether an entirely different direction is more promising. An iterative optimization loop may instead become very good at exploring the neighborhood of an existing solution and still remain stuck in a local optimum. So I'm curious about how people think about this distinction: How much scientific value is there in autonomous search over a human-defined research space? And what would an agent need, beyond better optimization, to demonstrate something closer to actual research judgment? submitted by /u/Only-Aardvark2568 [link] [comments]

items.title: OpenAI "rogue" agent activities found on Wikimedia projects [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI "rogue" agent activities found on Wikimedia projects Given how tempting a target wikis are for rogue agent swarms, it's not a huge surprise that Wikipedia found evidence of that activity once they went looking: The Wikimedia Foundation conducted its own investigation to see whether Wikimedia websites had been similarly affected by AI agents, focusing on those operated by OpenAI. We can confirm that we have discovered some activity by these "rogue" OpenAI agents on Wikimedia platforms. The unauthorized bot activities included edits to our wikis, some unsuccessful attempts to exploit a public note-taking tool we host, and heavy traffic, which are described more below. They found evidence of agents editing sandbox pages, trying to use pieces of infrastructure such as Etherpad to help proxy content from elsewhere, and saw widespread crawling and "hundreds of thousands of data queries" to their Wikidata Query Service. My best guess is that most of this was a similar (or the same) swarm of agents as those that defaced that German wiki while training for research tasks. The Wikipedia sandbox wiki edits appear to have started on May 12th, and the initial test edits to the UseModWiki Sandbox page reported by that incident started on May 11th. Tags: wikimedia, wikipedia, wikis, ai, generative-ai, llms, ai-ethics, accidental-cyberattacks
